masthead.title: Computer Chronicle
masthead.deck: The first August 1982 weekly: Commodore 64 reaches the retail moment, IBM PC clones gather, $100 computing gets real, and the arcade shelf keeps humming.

editorNote: Issue #1 starts the weekly run at Monday, August 2, 1982. The desk treats the week as a real 1982 newsstand bundle: date-specific where records are strong, same-month where period sources only pin the item to August.
morningLine: This week: the Commodore 64 reaches its August launch window, IBM PC momentum turns into a compatibility race, Timex puts a computer under $100, and rock radio has Eddie Money at number one.

lead.headline: Commodore 64 Reaches the August 1982 Retail Moment
lead.summary: The C64 is the home-computer story to circle this week: a 64K machine at a $595 introductory price, with TV hookup, BASIC, color graphics, sound, and room for disk drives, tape, modems, and printers. Guinness places the machine's manufacturing span from August 1982 to April 1994, while the Computer History Museum records its 64K memory and $595 cost. Exact store-by-store dates varied, so the issue labels this as the August 1982 launch window rather than a single-day debut.
lead.confidence: Month-specific launch window; exact day not asserted

computerItems.label: Commodore 64
computerItems.headline: 64K, SID Sound, VIC-II Color, and a Department-Store Future
computerItems.summary: The appeal is not just memory. The machine can use a family television, keeps BASIC close at hand, and arrives with a price meant to pressure Apple II, Atari 800, TI-99/4A, and TRS-80 buyers.

computerItems.label: Atari 8-bit
computerItems.headline: Atari 400/800 Owners Watch a New Rival Borrow Their Game-Computer Vocabulary
computerItems.summary: Atari still has strong color graphics, player-missile sprites, cartridge software, and a serious hobbyist base. The week's tension is that Commodore is now selling a cheaper 64K home machine into the same living-room lane.

computerItems.label: IBM PC / compatibles
computerItems.headline: The IBM PC Nears Its First Birthday With Clones Already Forming
computerItems.summary: IBM's own history says the PC was unveiled on August 12, 1981 and that by the end of 1982 retailers and software houses were rushing in. Columbia Data Products had already introduced a more-or-less IBM-compatible machine in June 1982, making compatibility a live buyer question this summer.
computerItems.confidence: Verified 1981 anniversary and June 1982 clone context

computerItems.label: Timex / Sinclair
computerItems.headline: The $99.95 Timex Sinclair 1000 Puts Computing Beside Watches and Drugstore Counters
computerItems.summary: Timex/Sinclair coverage said Americans would be able to buy the 2K machine in July through more than 100,000 retail outlets. By early August, under-$100 computing is no longer a mail-order curiosity; it is shelf bait for first-time BASIC learners.

computerItems.label: Storage & peripherals
computerItems.headline: Floppies, Tape, Printers, and Modems Define the Real Cost of Entry
computerItems.summary: The advertised computer price is only the opening bid. A useful 1982 setup often means a cassette recorder or 5.25-inch floppy drive, a TV or monitor, a printer for school or small business, and maybe a modem for CompuServe or The Source.
computerItems.confidence: Period-context synthesis from cited hardware descriptions

bbsNote.headline: Acoustic Couplers, 300 Baud Patience, and Long-Distance Bills
bbsNote.summary: A home modem remains a splurge, but the culture is forming: user groups, dial-up services, local bulletin boards, software swapping, and late-night phone discipline. For C64 and Atari owners, the modem is a future social life as much as a peripheral.

posts.text: Early buyers ask whether the real system needs cassette first or if saving for a 1541-style disk setup is the wiser move.
Atari owners compare graphics and game libraries against the new Commodore price pressure.
The $99.95 price turns computing into an impulse-counter topic, even if 2K RAM makes patience mandatory.

curiosity.headline: E.T. Keeps the Summer Box Office Orbiting the Suburbs
curiosity.summary: Spielberg's E.T. had opened June 11 and remained the broad pop-culture movie backdrop for early August. It fits this issue as the week's movie chatter, not as a computer story.
curiosity.confidence: Release verified; weekly box-office context broad

briefs.label: Magazine rack
briefs.headline: PC Magazine Moves Into Monthly Rhythm
briefs.summary: PC Magazine began 1982 as a specialist IBM PC title and moved to monthly publication with its August 1982 issue, another sign that the IBM PC had become its own magazine ecosystem.

briefs.label: Rock/pop crossover
briefs.headline: Survivor Still Owns Pop Radio While Rock Radio Picks Eddie Money
briefs.summary: On the August 7 Hot 100, Survivor's Eye of the Tiger remained number one; the dedicated weekly rock list put Eddie Money's Think I'm in Love on top.

briefs.label: Compatibility desk
briefs.headline: Workalike Is Not Always Compatible
briefs.summary: The IBM PC's open architecture is pulling in competitors, but 1982 buyers still need to ask whether software, disks, cards, and BIOS behavior actually line up.

periodAd.headline: Sunday Circular Watch: 64K Versus $99.95
periodAd.summary: Ask what comes in the box: BASIC in ROM, TV lead, cassette support, disk drive price, printer port, joystick ports, and whether the software shelf is already alive.
